passages.title: Cooling the Concrete City

source.doc: Bài mẫu do Claude viết (nội dung gốc, dùng tự do)
source.author: Claude

body: When the first thermometers were installed in London in the early nineteenth century, nobody expected them to reveal anything unusual about the city itself. Yet within a few decades, observers noticed that the centre of the capital was consistently warmer than the surrounding countryside, sometimes by as much as five degrees. This difference, now known as the urban heat island effect, has become one of the most studied features of modern cities.

The explanation is largely a matter of materials. Concrete, brick and asphalt absorb heat during the day and release it slowly after dark, which means that city streets often remain uncomfortably warm long after the sun has set. Dark roofs make the problem worse, and so does the lack of vegetation: plants cool the air by releasing water vapour, a process that paved surfaces cannot imitate. Heat from air conditioners, vehicles and industrial equipment adds further warmth.

For most of the twentieth century, planners treated this as a minor inconvenience. That attitude changed after the heatwave of 2003, which is estimated to have caused more than seventy thousand deaths across Europe. Elderly residents of dense inner-city districts were especially vulnerable, because their apartments, often on upper floors under dark roofs, could not shed heat at night. Since then, researchers have shown that the temperature gap between a city and its suburbs can double the risk of heat-related illness during extreme weather.

Planting trees is the most widely discussed remedy. A mature tree can reduce the temperature of the air beneath it by several degrees, and a continuous canopy along a street can lower surface temperatures even more. Trees also absorb rainwater, which reduces flooding, and they filter fine particles from the air. However, trees take decades to reach full size, and many cities lack the space to plant them in meaningful numbers. In some districts, underground cables and pipes make planting impossible.

Where trees cannot be planted, engineers have turned to the surfaces themselves. Reflective or 'cool' roofs, painted white or covered with light-coloured membranes, send most sunlight back into the sky instead of absorbing it. A trial in one southern European city found that buildings with such roofs were up to three degrees cooler inside during summer, which cut electricity use for cooling by about a fifth. Green roofs, planted with grass and shallow-rooted plants, work in a similar way but cost considerably more to install and maintain.

Critics point out that no single measure is enough. Reflective surfaces can create glare for pedestrians and, in winter, reduce the useful heat that buildings capture from the sun. Green roofs need regular watering, which is a problem in regions already short of water. Some researchers therefore argue that city governments should focus less on individual technologies and more on redesigning neighbourhoods as a whole, with wider streets for airflow, shaded public squares and open spaces connected by corridors of vegetation.

The cities that have made most progress share one feature: they set clear targets and measure results. One Asian metropolis now publishes a heat map of every district each summer, and uses it to decide where to plant trees first. Residents in the hottest areas are offered subsidies to repaint their roofs. Within eight years, the average summer night temperature in those districts fell by almost one degree. It is a modest figure, but experts consider it proof that deliberate planning can slow, if not reverse, a trend that was once regarded as unavoidable.

writingPrompts.text: Some people believe that city governments should spend public money on planting trees and creating parks, while others think the budget should go to improving public transport. Discuss both views and give your opinion.
writingPrompts.sampleAnswer:
Cities face many competing demands on their budgets. While some people argue that parks and trees deserve priority, others believe that public transport should come first. In my opinion, both matter, but a balanced approach that favours transport in the short term is more realistic.

Supporters of green spaces make a strong case. Trees absorb pollution, reduce flooding and lower summer temperatures, which can protect vulnerable residents during heatwaves. Parks also give people somewhere to exercise and relax, and this improves both physical and mental health. Moreover, these benefits are long-lasting, because a mature tree continues to serve the community for decades.

On the other hand, efficient public transport addresses problems that are more urgent for many commuters. Frequent buses and trains reduce traffic congestion, cut carbon emissions and make cities accessible to people who cannot afford a car. For a worker on a low income, a reliable bus route can mean access to better jobs, which is a significant social benefit that a park cannot provide.

Personally, I believe that transport deserves a larger share of funding at first, because it changes daily life immediately and reduces the number of cars that cause pollution in the first place. However, governments should not neglect greenery. Even modest investment, such as planting trees along new bus routes, can combine the advantages of both approaches.

In conclusion, although green spaces bring lasting environmental and health benefits, I think public transport should be the first priority, supported by smaller but steady spending on trees and parks.
